findings.title: The logistic-regression comparison accumulates likelihood precision in the baseline's prior, creating the reported large predictive gains
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2013__accepted__v14-wang13b-I01 — The logistic-regression comparison accumulates likelihood precision in the baseline's prior, creating the reported large predictive gains
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 17–20, Section 5.2 and Table 1 (printed pages 1021–1024), especially the claim on PDF page 19 that both proposed methods have much better log predictive likelihood and statistically outperform Jaakkola–Jordan inference. These results support the broader superiority claim in the introduction on PDF page 2 and discussion on PDF page 20. The concrete defect is in the footnoted author implementation: `logistic/logistic.py`, `Logistic_Regression.variational_logistic_regression`, original lines 44–51, particularly `S_inv = S0_inv` at line 49 followed by in-place additions. The software link is footnote 6 on PDF page 13.

**Claim.** With the same Bayesian logistic-regression model and fixed prior `mu0 = 0`, `Sigma0 = I`, the paper compares Laplace and delta inference with the Jaakkola–Jordan variational method. It uses a common score, the test-set average of `log sigmoid((2*z-1)*x.T*mu)`, and reports:

| Dataset | Jaakkola–Jordan accuracy / log score | Laplace | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Yeast | 79.7% / -0.678 | 80.1% / -0.449 | 80.2% / -0.450 |
| Scene | 87.4% / -0.670 | 89.4% / -0.259 | 89.5% / -0.265 |

The prose says that the proposed algorithms have slightly better accuracy, much better predictive likelihood, and significantly outperform the specialized method using a one-sided paired t-test across the independent binary classification problems. This empirical advantage is a stated justification for the new generic inference methods.

**Error and evidence.** The released baseline does not retain the specified prior precision. The relevant original code is:

```python
S0_inv = np.linalg.inv(S0)
mu_x = np.dot(S0_inv, mu0) + np.dot(train_data.labels_ - 0.5,
                                   train_data.features_)
while iter < max_iter:
    ...
    S_inv = S0_inv
    for i in range(num_samples):
        S_inv += 2 * lambda_var_params[i] * np.outer(
            train_data.features_[i, :], train_data.features_[i, :])
```

NumPy assignment aliases the array. Therefore the in-place `+=` operations mutate `S0_inv` itself. The correct Jaakkola–Jordan Gaussian precision update is

\[
S_t^{-1}=\Sigma_0^{-1}+2\sum_n\lambda(\xi_{n,t})x_nx_n^\top,
\qquad
\lambda(\xi)=\frac{\sigma(\xi)-1/2}{2\xi}.
\]

The implemented update instead retains every preceding iteration's likelihood contribution:

\[
S_{t,\mathrm{code}}^{-1}
=\Sigma_0^{-1}
 +2\sum_{r=1}^{t}\sum_n\lambda(\xi_{n,r})x_nx_n^\top.
\]

The linear term `mu_x` is computed once. In the paper's zero-prior-mean setting, the baseline coefficient mean consequently shrinks toward zero as iterations accumulate, and its predictive probabilities approach one half. The very poor near-`-log(2)` scores are a consequence of this artificial precision accumulation, rather than evidence that the specified specialized variational method gives those predictions. The mathematical repair is exactly:

```python
S_inv = S0_inv.copy()
```

I tested this repair on the original Mulan Yeast and Scene training/test splits, using every one of the 14 and 6 binary tasks, respectively. The feature counts and sample counts match the paper: Yeast 103 features, 1500/917 samples; Scene 294 features, 1211/1196 samples. I appended the intercept exactly as the author's data reader does, retained `mu0=0`, `Sigma0=I`, used the same initialization for each paired method, and evaluated the same explicit predictive score for all methods. The author routines were run after Python 2 syntax/runtime compatibility changes; the baseline repair changes only the aliasing line. At the released driver's default 50 iterations the results are:

| Dataset | Original baseline | Copy-repaired baseline | Native Laplace | Native delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Yeast accuracy | 0.796775 | 0.801449 | 0.801293 | 0.801683 |
| Yeast log score | -0.684387 | -0.449146 | -0.448984 | -0.449507 |
| Scene accuracy | 0.873328 | 0.894788 | 0.893534 | 0.895485 |
| Scene log score | -0.679498 | -0.264807 | -0.259046 | -0.265239 |

The repaired baseline has *higher* accuracy than Laplace on both datasets. Delta's remaining accuracy differences are not significant under the paper's test. The Yeast predictive advantage vanishes; delta's predictive score is slightly worse than the corrected baseline on both datasets at 50 iterations. **Laplace's Scene log-score advantage survives**, and is not claimed to be false.

This result is not an artifact of stopping the repaired baseline too early. An independently implemented fixed-prior Jaakkola–Jordan iteration was continued until the relative change of its actual variational bound was below `1e-11` (at most 187 iterations on Yeast and 486 on Scene). Its aggregate accuracy/log score was `0.801449 / -0.449146` on Yeast and `0.894788 / -0.265368` on Scene. The bound increased throughout. Using these converged baselines and the same per-label one-sided test as the paper gives:

| Proposed method / metric | Yeast mean difference, p | Scene mean difference, p |
|---|---:|---:|
| Laplace accuracy | -0.000156, 0.750 | -0.001254, 0.905 |
| Laplace log score | +0.000163, 0.177 | +0.006322, **0.00130** |
| Delta accuracy | +0.000234, 0.168 | +0.000697, 0.129 |
| Delta log score | -0.000361, 0.906 | +0.000129, 0.467 |

Thus seven of the eight method/dataset/metric superiority contrasts suggested by the prose do not survive a correct baseline in the controlled reproduction. Table 1 already prints the Scene/delta likelihood cell without bold emphasis; I do not claim that all eight cells are explicitly marked significant in the table. Over 98% of the large Laplace-versus-baseline likelihood gaps in the 50-iteration reproduction disappears; the Yeast accuracy ranking reverses, as does the Scene Laplace accuracy ranking. These are consequences of a specific defective comparator, rather than a request for additional experiments.

**Provenance and reproducibility.** The exact archive named in footnote 6 was recovered at the author's CMU AFS location, because the ordinary homepage URL now redirects:

`https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/user/chongw/www/software/nonconjugate_inference.tar.gz`

It has 10,689 bytes and SHA-256 `2ba9e2708631986f39c872cf12d94fadf4768d7fbb100dc107be17df100e952f`. Its internal `logistic.zip` timestamps the relevant source May 20, 2012, before publication. Dataset files came from the Mulan maintainer's repository, under `tsoumakas/mulan/data/multi-label/{yeast,scene}/`; exact download URLs and SHA-256 hashes are saved in `dataset-retrieval.json`.

The evidence directory is:

`[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`

It contains:

- The original archive and extracted author source, plus separate compatibility copies in `native_py3/`.
- `wangb-logistic-control.py`: the native paired experiment, including the single-line corrected module; `native-logistic-results.json` and `native-outputs/*.npz`: per-label scores, coefficient means and covariances for all four methods.
- `wangb-jj-vector.py` and `vectorized-jj-results.json`: an independent matrix-form implementation of both original and corrected updates. Its 50-iteration means agree with native coefficient vectors to less than `9e-12`.
- `wangb-jj-converged.py`, `converged-jj-results.json`, and `converged-paired-statistics.json`: the converged baseline and paired checks; `paired-statistics.json` retains the 50-iteration version.

The native experiment can be reproduced with NumPy/SciPy by running `wangb-logistic-control.py` from this directory, adjusting its recorded absolute evidence/SciPy paths if moved. The independent checks provide a second route without relying on the driver's update implementation.

I do **not** claim to have recovered the exact historical five random starts, cross-validation assignments, or all table-generation logs. The native experiment above uses one shared initialization per label and the original provided fixed train/test splits. As a separate historical consistency check, the erroneous implementation at 30 iterations gives aggregate accuracy/log score `0.797087 / -0.678556` for Yeast and `0.874303 / -0.669856` for Scene, close to the published baseline entries. The Laplace/delta aggregates also agree with the table at its displayed precision. These observations support the linkage to the published comparison; they are not represented as exact recovery of the original runs.

**Reason for rejection.** A main empirical contribution is that the new generic approximations outperform inference designed specifically for these models. Table 1 and its significance claims are central evidence for that contribution in Bayesian logistic regression. They compare the new methods against an implementation whose effective prior changes every iteration, rather than the specified Jaakkola–Jordan method under the common fixed prior. Correcting the baseline largely eliminates the reported likelihood improvement and removes most of the stated statistical superiority, including all delta-inference superiority in this controlled experiment. Consequently the paper's reported comparative conclusion and its explanation in terms of better posterior inference are unsupported as written. A journal referee should reject that claimed empirical demonstration pending replacement of the comparisons and revision of the conclusions. Although the code fix is one line, it does **not** preserve the central reported result, so this is not a routine correction below the requested threshold.

This finding does not refute the generic Laplace/delta framework, invalidate the separate CTM experiment, or erase the surviving Scene Laplace log-score advantage. Those limits do not restore the failed main logistic-regression comparison.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Table 1's unusually weak near-one-half baseline probabilities, I inspected the recovered baseline precision update and noticed assignment followed by in-place modification of the prior array.

**Verification method.** I rechecked the original PDF's common prior, predictive metric, reported results and significance procedure, including rendered PDF pages 20–21. I authenticated the footnoted prepublication software, derived the fixed-prior precision update and the accumulated-precision recurrence, ran all 20 original binary tasks with native and single-line repaired code, independently reproduced the updates in matrix form, and checked converged fixed-prior inference and the paper's own paired test.

**Confidence: High.** The aliasing mechanism is exact and the repair is isolated; native and independent numerical implementations agree, original dataset sizes and reported accuracy/likelihood patterns align, and the corrected comparison changes materially. Exact historical random starts are unavailable, so the numerical claim is scoped to the fully specified controlled reproduction rather than asserting bitwise reproduction of every published entry. Independent bounded referee QA agreed that the demonstrated baseline flaw crosses the accept-to-reject threshold.
